checks.name: Runs test (is the sequence random?)
checks.detail: 15,513 runs vs 14,970 expected (z = +6.28, p = 0.000): more switches than chance: results tend to alternate. Check that it also holds out of sample.

checks.name: Does one result predict the next?
checks.detail: lag-1 correlation -0.0363 (z = -6.29). Statistically non-zero, but check its size: a correlation this small moves the next window's odds by only about 1.8 percentage points, less than fees cost.

checks.name: Hour-of-day lean holds out of sample?
checks.detail: Split at 2026-06-16. Hours that looked significant in the first half: none; still significant, same direction, in the second half: none. Correlation of hourly leans between halves: -0.23 (near zero: the hourly pattern is noise).

checks.name: Streak behaviour holds out of sample?
checks.detail: after 3 Ups the next was Up 46.3% (first half, n=1,643) vs 47.5% (second half, n=1,707); after 3 Downs the next was Up 53.7% (first half, n=1,662) vs 53.7% (second half, n=1,745). For a fade-or-follow rule to pay, the same lean must show in both halves and be larger than the ~2–3¢ per contract that spread and fees cost.

checks.name: Kalshi price edge holds out of sample?
checks.detail: 1 price level looked clearly profitable in the first half (buy Yes at 70–80¢) but did not hold up in the second. 7 more showed a paper profit that sits inside its error band, so it could just be luck: buy No at 40–50¢: +11.1¢ ±11.2 (n=70); buy No at 30–40¢: +6.9¢ ±12.4 (n=51); buy Yes at 20–30¢: +4.2¢ ±10.0 (n=85). Most windows trade under 10¢ or over 90¢; there, recent results ran -0.4¢ to -0.1¢ per contract.

checks.name: Chance findings to expect
checks.detail: The report tests 35 hour, weekday and slot groups; at 95% confidence about 1.8 would look significant by luck alone. Found: 0. That's no more than luck would produce.
